Participants noted that recent data on spending had been strong, supported by a strong job market and rising incomes, with some commenting that contacts in their Districts remained optimistic about consumer spending [2019-01-30/participantsViews/3]. They also observed that labor market conditions had remained strong, with payrolls growing at an above-trend rate and elevated labor market tightness [2018-12-19/participantsViews/8]. Wage costs rose 3.0% over the year, and average hourly earnings increased 3.2% over the year [2019-05-01]. However, no specific discussion of wages or compensation was found in the minutes.

Several participants noted that the foreign exchange value of the U.S. dollar had fallen back somewhat over the intermeeting period, though it had increased significantly since the middle of last year and was seen as likely to continue restraining U.S. economic activity [2015-04-29/participantsViews/5]. During discussions on foreign economic outlooks, participants observed that the dollar had appreciated, especially against the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling, and some expressed concern about this trend [2014-09-17/participantsViews/9]. The broad U.S. dollar index was 105.8 on 2015-05-22, down from 105.5 three months earlier and 93.69 a year earlier [the broad U.S. dollar index].

Between 2010 and 2012, the Committee's view of the housing market improved. In 2010, participants noted the housing sector remained depressed, with foreclosures increasing supply and putting downward pressure on prices and construction [2010-11-03/participantsViews/4]. By 2012, the Committee saw a pickup in housing markets, with household spending and housing improvements offsetting a slowdown in the business sector [2012-10-23/policyAction/1]. The Committee also changed its reinvestment policy to support mortgage markets by shifting funds to agency MBS [2011-09-21/policyAction/2]. Overall, the view shifted from deep depression to gradual recovery.

Between 2017 and 2019, the Committee viewed labor market conditions as strengthening. In December 2017, the Committee raised the federal funds rate target to 1-1/4 to 1-1/2 percent, noting strong labor market conditions and inflation expectations [2017-12-13/policyAction/12]. By December 2018, labor market conditions were described as continuing to strengthen, with solid job gains and real GDP growth [2018-12-19/staffEconomy/1]. In October 2019, participants judged labor market conditions as strong, with unemployment near historical lows and continued solid job gains [2019-10-30/participantsViews/6].
